text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- Equal women's rights will become part of Austria's constitution. The government coalition will now work out ways of implementing the demands of a petition on more women's rights.

- The Styrian conservative People's Party says Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel is moving in the right direction in his bid for Austria to join NATO even if parts of the party remain sceptical of this move.

- Opposition Greens say Vienna's former mayor Helmut Zilk's pressure on the Interior Ministry was the start of the affair around the release of the alleged Iranian murderers of three Kurdish leaders in 1989.
- Interior Minister Karl Schloegl urges Russia to give information on where the Soviet KGB's arms depots are.
- Over the next three years Post & Telekom Austria plans to let 6,500 postmen retire early in a bid to reduce the company's number of employees it has agreed with the Finance Ministry.
- The energy industry is against plans by Economics Minister Hannes Farnleitner to introduce more competitivity within the Austrian energy sector in a bid to prepare it for liberalisation.
- Transport Minister Caspar Einem and Economics Minister Farnleitner have agreed on a draft telecommunications law after weeks of discussion between the Social Democrats and Conservatives.

- Car engineer Steyr-Daimler-Puch will pay a dividend of six schillings for the first time in five years after it reported a pretax profit of 86 million schillings from a loss of 80 million the year before. The group plans to buy back the 50 percent stake in its engineering unit Fahrzeugtechnik from its parent Creditanstalt.
- Austrians are ranked sixth within the EU for paying back loans in time.
- Austria plans to invest in the rebuilding of Lebanon and Syria.
- Raiffeisenlandesbank Niederoesterreich-Wien plans to raise its market share in Vienna by 50 percent after the Vienna and Lower Austrian units merged earlier this year.
DIE PRESSE
- Social Minister Lore Hostasch is against plans to reduce social spending saying there is no necessity for it.
- Austria's mint Muenze Oesterreich will invest 300 million schillings in modernising its production facilities in preparation for the introduction of Europe's single currency euro.
- The European Commission will not subsidise investments worth 300 million schilings by chemicals group Hoffmann-La Roche in Linz, upper Austria, thereby jeopardising the future of the plant.
- Austria Tabak's sales monopoly is threatened by the European Commission which plans take legal action against it.

- Gerhard Randa, chief of Bank Austria, takes over as supervisory board chief of brickmaker Wienerberger from former Creditanstalt chief Guido Schmidt-Chiari. Bank Austria took over the government's stake in Creditanstalt at the beginning of the year.
- Chancellor Viktor Klima has said Austria would freeze all accounts of Zairean ex-dictator Mobutu although no accounts have actually been found yet.
KURIER
- Parliament will decide on lowering the blood-alcohol level to 0.05 percent for car drivers while conservative party leaders say it is not necessary to reduce it from 0.08 percent.
- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger expects pensions will not be raised by more than one percent for 1998.
- Social Democrats demand a social grading of agricultural subsidies by the European Union.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- Insurer EA Generali and Creditanstalt are talking about closing their ties after Bank Austria's takeover of the latter.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- European Union says Austria is not yet allowed to include illicit work in the country's gross domestic product (GDP).
- Upper Austria plans to privatise 25 percent of the state's energy provider OKA by the end of the year.
